text.p: Gold miner Newcrest Mining Ltd on Thursday reported a higher half-year net profit and unburdened itself of a troubled investment in fellow gold miner Normandy Mining Ltd.
Newcrest's net profit came in at A$15.8 million, up 32 percent on a year ago.
However a A$9.5 million net abnormal gain masked the effect of falling output and higher costs on pre-abnormal profits which fell to A$6.3 million, just shy of market expectations.

The abnormals gathered an A$172.8 million profit from gold hedging closeouts and A$1.8 million from the sale of the Ora Banda mine in Western Australia and pitted them against a A$134.7 million writedown in its 11.9 percent stake in Normandy.

While counting the cost of the paper losses in Normandy, Newcrest also unveiled a novel two-year gold swap which saw it offload its stake to Australia and New Zealand Banking Group in a deal which valued each Normandy share at A$1.75.
The price also ruled off Newcrest's losses on Normandy at about A$113 million since March, when it tried to deal itself a place in the merger between Normandy and its subsidiaries.
Analysts hailed the A$337 million deal as releasing Newcrest from the short-term constraints of holding the Normandy shares and associated debt.

"The deal with ANZ is very positive given that it removes for Newcrest a situation where it had some debt against the investment and tidies up their balance sheet," said ANZ Securities resource analyst David Kauler.
"It's good for Newcrest and allows them ... to raise further debt to go ahead with their capital expansion."
Macquarie Equities gold analyst Grant Craighead said: "It's good they finalised the Normandy transaction, that is a positive as it removes some doubt and risk from the market."

The swap allowed Newcrest to repay the A$200 million of debt which funded its A$450 million Normandy play and left it with A$130 million to plough into future investments such as the A$440 million Cadia mine in New South Wales or Gosawong project in Indonesia.
But the deal did not protect Newcrest from Thursday's Australian share market torpor which left the company's shares two cents lower at A$4.88 by the close.
Newcrest posted a A$20.81 million net profit for the year to June 30, 1996.
The company's main operating troubles stem from continued lower grades and leach pad problems at its main mine, Telfer in Western Australia.
The problems at the mine, which Newcrest announced was under review, has been compounded by persistent heavy rains which have forced a two-week closure.
